title: India Just Rewired Its Entire Oil Supply Chain. Venezuela Is Now Its Fifth-Largest Crude Supplier.
excerpt: With the Strait of Hormuz closed for three months, India's refiners have pivoted to Latin America, Africa, and the UAE at extraordinary speed. The import map that existed in January no longer exists.
body:
Three months ago, India's crude oil import map looked like it had for years: Russia on top, followed by Iraq, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, with smaller volumes from Africa and the Americas.

That map no longer exists.

The closure of the Strait of Hormuz — through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil and LNG supply once flowed — has forced India's refiners into the most dramatic supply-chain pivot in the country's energy history. And the speed of the shift has surprised even industry veterans.

## The New Oil Map

According to shipping data and industry sources compiled by Reuters, India's oil imports now look radically different:

The UAE has surged to 45.2 percent of India's total oil imports in April, up from roughly 15 percent before the war. Abu Dhabi's Murban crude, which bypasses the Strait of Hormuz via the Fujairah pipeline, has become India's most critical lifeline.

Russia's share has fallen to around 35 percent, down from over 40 percent — not because Russia is unwilling to sell, but because tanker routes from Russia's Pacific ports are stretched thin and insurance costs have spiked.

Venezuela, barely a factor in India's import ledger a year ago, has become India's fifth-largest crude supplier. Brazilian and Nigerian crude are also flowing in volumes that would have been unthinkable before the war.

## Why It Matters

India imports about 85 percent of its crude oil — roughly 5 million barrels per day. Every disruption to supply routes translates directly into higher fuel prices, wider trade deficits, and inflationary pressure on an economy of 1.4 billion people.

The Hormuz closure didn't just reduce supply — it rerouted it. Ships that once took 3-5 days from Gulf ports to Indian refineries now take 15-25 days from West Africa or Latin America. Longer routes mean more tankers tied up in transit, higher freight costs, and larger working capital requirements for refiners.

Indian refiners have responded with remarkable pragmatism. Reliance Industries, which operates the world's largest refining complex at Jamnagar, Gujarat, has reportedly signed new term contracts with Nigerian and Angolan producers. Indian Oil Corporation and Bharat Petroleum have diversified their spot purchases across a dozen new suppliers.

## The UAE Lifeline

The single biggest beneficiary of India's pivot has been the UAE. The Fujairah oil terminal, located on the Gulf of Oman outside the Strait of Hormuz, has become the most strategically important piece of energy infrastructure for India's oil security.

Abu Dhabi's ADNOC has ramped up production and pipeline flows to Fujairah, which can load tankers without passing through the contested strait. India's imports from the UAE nearly tripled between February and April, making the Emirates India's largest single-country supplier for the first time.

The relationship is deepening beyond crude. India and the UAE signed a comprehensive economic partnership agreement in 2022, and the current crisis has accelerated energy cooperation. Indian strategic petroleum reserves are being topped up with Murban crude.

## What India Lost

The reshuffling has come at a steep cost. India's total oil import bill has risen an estimated 35 to 40 percent compared to the same period last year, driven by both higher crude prices (Brent at $90-96 per barrel) and higher freight costs.

The rupee has weakened to 95.68 against the dollar, partly due to the ballooning trade deficit. Petrol has crossed ₹100 per liter in most Indian cities after four price hikes in two weeks. The Reserve Bank of India is now expected to raise interest rates by up to 100 basis points to contain war-driven inflation.

Roughly 100,000 tonnes of Indian rice earmarked for Gulf markets remain stuck at ports, unable to ship through the Hormuz chokepoint. Mango exports, fertilizer imports, and LNG supplies have all been disrupted.

## The Permanent Shift?

Energy analysts say some of India's supply-chain changes may outlast the war. Refiners who have built relationships with Venezuelan, Nigerian, and Brazilian producers may continue those arrangements even after Hormuz reopens — as a hedge against future disruptions.

"India learned in three months what took Europe two years after Russia's invasion of Ukraine," one Mumbai-based energy consultant told Reuters. "The diversification was forced, but it won't be fully reversed."

The question now is whether a U.S.-Iran deal materializes. Iran said Wednesday it had obtained a draft framework that would restore commercial shipping through Hormuz within a month, but Trump dismissed the report and the U.S. military launched fresh strikes near Bandar Abbas hours later.

Until the strait reopens, India's new oil map is the only one that matters.
author: Diaspora Desk
